newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT -Dlr/yen eyes further downside test.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT -Dlr/yen eyes further downside test.

text.p: The U.S. currency's failure this week to break above October's 1996 high of 114.92 yen combined with weakness in the mark/yen cross could put further downside pressure on dollar/yen, chartists said.
Joseph Klettner, a foreign exchange analyst at Chase Securities Inc, noted that dollar/yen put in an important double top, with peaks at 114.92 and 114.80.
Klettner said he expects the dollar to continue downward and retest 110.62 yen, a low from November 15.
He pegged interim support at 112.62 yen, adding a break of that level would confirm the double top is in place.b
The dollar slid to 113.05/10 yen at 1600 EST/2100 GMT, down from 113.27/37 at the open. The German currency also weakened against the yen.
Crosscurrents Investment Advisory President Keith Raphael placed the U.S. currency in a tight short-term range from 112.70 to 113.35 yen.
He said dollar/yen will remain "heavy" because of pressure from mark/yen.
But Raphael also said, "I don't see anything very negative happening in the short-term that will send the dollar back below 1.54 (marks) or below 112 (yen)."
The dollar also fell versus the mark, trading at 1.5600/10 marks at 1600 EST/2100 GMT compared with 1.5610/20 at the open.
Chartists, however, predicted the dollar will resume its rally against the mark.
Raphael said his year-end price objective for dollar/mark since last February has been 1.5890 marks. Furthermore, he said he expects the dollar at 1.64 marks in mid-January.
"I'm still extremely bullish and anticipate a continued strong dollar...," Raphael said.
Meanwhile, Klettner sketched good dollar support at 1.5556 marks with resistance on Wednesday at 1.5680.
He deemed 1.5454 marks as the maximum level the dollar will pull back to if there is further corrective action from this week's high of 1.5735.
On a slightly longer term basis, Klettner said the dollar could climb to 1.58 to 1.59 marks before undergoing a much more significant consolidation.
